A leave-taking is the act of saying goodbye — but not just any goodbye. It is a deliberate, conscious farewell, the moment when someone formally parts from another person, a place, or a stage of life. It is the act itself: the goodbye, the parting, the departure.

Think of it this way: when you "take your leave," you are formally signalling that you are about to go. A leave-taking is that entire act — the goodbye ritual, the parting moment.
What makes it different from just "goodbye"

The word "goodbye" is something you can say in a split second, even casually. A leave-taking is bigger than that. It carries weight. It implies that the parting matters — that the separation is meaningful, significant, or emotionally felt. It is the kind of farewell you pause for. The kind where something is at stake.

It also has a slightly formal and literary flavour. You would not use it in casual speech the way you say "bye" to a friend. You would more likely encounter it in writing, in thoughtful speech, or when describing a parting of real consequence.

A leave-taking is almost always tinged with feeling — sadness, tenderness, solemnity, or bittersweetness. It suggests that the people involved are aware of what this goodbye means. It could be:

  • The last time two people will see each other for a long while
  • A final farewell before death or a great loss
  • A ceremonial departure (a retirement, a graduation, a soldier going to war)
  • An emotionally loaded goodbye that both people feel deeply

This is why you would not say "We had a quick leave-taking at the door" — the word itself implies it was not quick or trivial. The moment had presence.

You can use it with articles and make it plural:

  • a leave-taking (one such event)
  • the leave-taking (a specific one you are referring to)
  • leave-takings (many such farewells)

1. The leave-taking at the airport was tearful — none of them knew when they would see each other again.

Here, the farewell at the airport is an emotionally heavy, significant parting. The word captures that weight.

2. He had rehearsed the leave-taking in his mind many times, but when the moment arrived, he found he had nothing to say.

This shows how a leave-taking is a defined moment — anticipated, prepared for, felt.

3. After twenty years of service, her leave-taking from the company was marked with speeches and quiet gratitude.

Here it refers to a formal, ceremonial departure from a phase of life — her retirement or resignation.

4. Their leave-takings were always long — neither of them was good at endings.

This plural use shows that a pattern of drawn-out farewells defines the relationship.

5. The novel ends with a quiet leave-taking, the protagonist walking away without looking back.

Here the word appears in a literary context, describing a final, deliberate departure.

Leave-taking is sometimes used metaphorically — not about parting from a person, but from something abstract: a way of life, a belief, an era, a version of oneself.

  • His move to the city felt like a leave-taking from everything he had ever known.
  • The last chapter of the book is a leave-taking from innocence.

In these cases, the word signals a conscious, felt departure from something — not a physical goodbye, but a meaningful ending.
When would you actually use this word?

You would reach for leave-taking when you want to convey that a farewell was:

  • Significant and emotionally weighted
  • Deliberate and conscious, not offhand
  • Formal, ceremonial, or memorable
  • Worth pausing and naming as an event in itself

If a departure was trivial, rushed, or unfeeling, leave-taking would feel like the wrong word — it would sound oddly grand. But when a goodbye has real weight, this word carries it precisely.
A leave-taking is a meaningful, often emotionally charged act of parting — a farewell that both the one leaving and the one left behind recognise as significant.
